# Summary

# Introduction

**Does flipper length or body mass more accurately classify penguin species (Adélie, Chinstrap, Gentoo)?**

## Background

The Palmer Penguins dataset (Horst et al., 2020) contains body measurements of adult Adélie, Chinstrap and Gentoo penguins (genus *Pygoscelis*) nesting on three islands in Antarctica's Palmer Archipelago: Biscoe, Dream and Torgersen. The data were collected from 2007 to 2009 by Dr. Kristen Gorman and the Palmer Station Antarctica Long Term Ecological Research (LTER) program, as part of a study of differences between male and female penguins.

Every breeding season, researchers identified studies nests where pairs of adults were present prior to egg-laying and consistently monitored these sites. Once a nest was found to have one egg, both adults were captured, measured, and had a blood sample taken to determine each penguin's sex (Gorman et al., 2014). Consequently, every observation in the data set represents a breeding adult measured at the same point in the nesting cycle.

## Relevance

Exploring how flipper length and body mass independently relates to penguin species is valuable because the two measurements describe very different kinds of traits. Flipper length is structural: once a penguin is fully grown, it stays roughly constant. In comparison, body mass varies based on factors like foraging success and breeding effort, so it reflects a penguin's current condition as much as its species. Finding out which one better separates the species tells us whether species differences are better captured by stable body structure or by size that fluctuates, which matters for any study that compares penguins measured at different times or under different conditions.

## Data Description

We use the `penguins` data set from the `palmerpenguins` package (Horst et al., 2020), which contains 344 penguins: 152 Adélie, 68 Chinstrap and 124 Gentoo. Each row represents one adult penguin and records its species, island, bill length, bill depth, flipper length, body mass, sex and study year. Our analysis uses three of these variables:

- `species`: penguin species (Adélie, Chinstrap or Gentoo); the target we classify.
- `flipper_length_mm`: flipper length, in millimetres.
- `body_mass_g`: body mass, in grams.

Two penguins have no flipper length or body mass recorded, so we remove them before analysis. The remaining variables are not used.

# Methods

## Data Collection

We used the Palmer Penguins dataset, which contains measurements and species information for penguins observed in the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica. The dataset was obtained from the publicly available GitHub repository maintained by the Palmer Penguins project (Horst et al., 2020).

We focused on three variables: penguin species, flipper length, and body mass. Species was used as the response variable, while flipper length and body mass were evaluated separately as predictors.

```{python}
# Create data directories
raw_dir = Path("../data/raw")
processed_dir = Path("../data/processed")

raw_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
processed_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

# Download the original dataset
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/allisonhorst/palmerpenguins/main/inst/extdata/penguins.csv"
raw_data = pd.read_csv(url)

# Save the original dataset
raw_data.to_csv(raw_dir / "penguins.csv", index=False)

# Select relevant variables and remove missing values
data = raw_data[
    ["species", "flipper_length_mm", "body_mass_g"]
].dropna()

# Save processed data
data.to_csv(processed_dir / "penguins_cleaned.csv", index=False)
```

## Traing-Test Splitting

We divided the cleaned dataset into training and testing sets using a 75:25 ratio. We performed this split before exploratory data analysis and preprocessing to prevent information from the test set from influencing model development.

```{python}

train_data, test_data = train_test_split(
    data,
    test_size=0.25,
    random_state=123,
    stratify=data["species"]
)

# Separate response variable and predictors
y_train = train_data["species"]
y_test = test_data["species"]

X_train_flipper = train_data[["flipper_length_mm"]]
X_test_flipper = test_data[["flipper_length_mm"]]

X_train_mass = train_data[["body_mass_g"]]
X_test_mass = test_data[["body_mass_g"]]
```

## Exploratory Data Analysis

We explored the training data to understand how flipper length and body mass vary across the three penguin species. We calculated descriptive statistics and created boxplots to examine differences between species and identify potential overlap in their measurements.

```{python}
# Descriptive statistics
summary_stats = train_data.groupby("species")[
    ["flipper_length_mm", "body_mass_g"]
].agg(["count", "mean", "std"])
summary_stats
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-penguin-flipper-length
#| fig-cap: "Flipper Length of penguins by species."

# Visualize measurements by species
# Flipper length by species
flipper_chart = alt.Chart(train_data).mark_boxplot().encode(
    y=alt.Y("species:N", title="Penguin Species"),
    x=alt.X("flipper_length_mm:Q", title="Flipper Length (mm)"),
    color=alt.Color("species:N", title="Species")
).properties(
    title="Flipper Length by Penguin Species"
)
flipper_chart
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-penguin-body-mass
#| fig-cap: "Body Mass of penguins by species."
# Body mass by species
mass_chart = alt.Chart(train_data).mark_boxplot().encode(
    y=alt.Y("species:N", title="Penguin Species"),
    x=alt.X("body_mass_g:Q", title="Body Mass (g)"),
    color=alt.Color("species:N", title="Species")
).properties(
    title="Body Mass by Penguin Species"
)
mass_chart
```

## Model Training

We used logistic regression to classify penguins into three species: Adélie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo with\
Logistic regression is a classification method that estimates the probability of an observation belonging to each class.

To compare the predictive ability of the two measurements, we developed two separate models:

Flipper length model: uses flipper length as the only predictor.

Body mass model: uses body mass as the only predictor.

Both models used the same training and testing sets. We standardized the predictor variables using StandardScaler within a pipeline. This ensures that the scaling parameters are learned from the training data only.

```{python}
# Model 1: Flipper length
flipper_model = make_pipeline(
    StandardScaler(),
    LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)
)

flipper_model.fit(X_train_flipper, y_train)
```

```{python}
# Model 2: Body mass
mass_model = make_pipeline(
    StandardScaler(),
    LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)
)

mass_model.fit(X_train_mass, y_train)
```

## Model Evaluation

We evaluated both models using accuracy and macro-averaged F1-score on the test set. Accuracy measures the proportion of correctly classified penguins. However, because the number of observations may differ across species, accuracy alone may not fully represent classification performance.

The macro-averaged F1-score considers both precision and recall and calculates the average F1-score across all three species, giving each species equal weight. This allows us to assess how well each model performs across the different classes.

We also used confusion matrices to examine which species were correctly classified and which were misclassified.

```{python}

# Generate test-set predictions using the fitted pipelines
y_pred_flipper = flipper_model.predict(X_test_flipper)
y_pred_mass = mass_model.predict(X_test_mass)

# Build clean summary comparison table
results_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Predictor": ["Flipper Length", "Body Mass"],
    "Overall Accuracy": [
        round(accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred_flipper), 3),
        round(accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred_mass), 3),
    ],
    "Macro Precision": [
        round(precision_score(y_test, y_pred_flipper, average="macro", zero_division=0), 3),
        round(precision_score(y_test, y_pred_mass, average="macro", zero_division=0), 3),
    ],
    "Macro Recall": [
        round(recall_score(y_test, y_pred_flipper, average="macro", zero_division=0), 3),
        round(recall_score(y_test, y_pred_mass, average="macro", zero_division=0), 3),
    ],
    "Macro F1-Score": [
        round(f1_score(y_test, y_pred_flipper, average="macro", zero_division=0), 3),
        round(f1_score(y_test, y_pred_mass, average="macro", zero_division=0), 3),
    ],
})
```

# Results

To evaluate whether flipper length or body mass more accurately classifies penguin species, both fitted logistic regression models were evaluated on the held-out test set ($n = 86$). Table 1 compares the overall test accuracy alongside macro averaged precision, recall, and F1-score for each single-predictor model.

```{python}
results_table.style.hide(axis="index").format({
    "Overall Accuracy": "{:.3f}",
    "Macro Precision": "{:.3f}",
    "Macro Recall": "{:.3f}",
    "Macro F1-Score": "{:.3f}",
})
```

Table 1. Held-out test set classification performance comparing single-predictor logistic regression models using flipper length versus body mass across overall accuracy and macro averaged precision, recall, and F1-score.

As shown in Table 1, flipper length outperformed body mass across every evaluation metric. The flipper length classifier achieved an overall test accuracy of 0.837 and a macro-averaged F1-score of 0.715, compared to an overall accuracy of 0.744 and a macro-averaged F1-score of 0.561 for the body mass classifier.

```{python}
species_order = ["Adelie", "Chinstrap", "Gentoo"]

def build_cm_df(y_true, y_pred, model_label):
    cm = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred, labels=species_order)
    rows = []
    for i, actual in enumerate(species_order):
        for j, predicted in enumerate(species_order):
            rows.append({
                "Model": model_label,
                "Actual Species": actual,
                "Predicted Species": predicted,
                "Count": int(cm[i, j]),
            })
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

cm_combined = pd.concat([
    build_cm_df(y_test, y_pred_flipper, "Flipper Length Model"),
    build_cm_df(y_test, y_pred_mass, "Body Mass Model"),
], ignore_index=True)

base = alt.Chart(cm_combined).encode(
    x=alt.X("Predicted Species:N", sort=species_order, title="Predicted Species"),
    y=alt.Y("Actual Species:N", sort=species_order, title="Actual Species"),
)

heatmap = base.mark_rect().encode(
    color=alt.Color("Count:Q", scale=alt.Scale(scheme="blues"), title="Penguin Count")
)

text = base.mark_text(fontSize=13, fontWeight="bold").encode(
    text="Count:Q",
    color=alt.condition(
        alt.datum.Count > 15,
        alt.value("white"),
        alt.value("black"),
    ),
)

cm_chart = (heatmap + text).properties(
    width=220,
    height=220,
).facet(
    column=alt.Column(
        "Model:N",
        sort=["Flipper Length Model", "Body Mass Model"],
        title=None,
        header=alt.Header(labelFontSize=13, labelFontWeight="bold"),
    )
).configure_axis(
    labelFontSize=11,
    titleFontSize=12,
)

cm_chart
```

Figure 3. Side-by-side confusion matrices comparing actual versus predicted penguin species on the held-out test set for the flipper length logistic regression model (left) and the body mass logistic regression model (right).

Figure 3 illustrates how each predictor separates the three penguin species on the test set. Both models reliably identified Gentoo penguins, reflecting their noticeably longer flippers and larger body mass relative to the other two species. However, substantial overlap between Adélie and Chinstrap penguins limited single feature classification performance, with the body mass model misclassifying almost all Chinstrap penguins as Adélie, whereas flipper length provided moderately stronger separation between those two smaller species.

# Discussion

*Pygoscelis adeliae* (Adélie), *Pygoscelis papua* (Gentoo), and *Pygoscelis antarcticus* (Chinstrap) are three species of brush-tailed penguins residing in the Antarctic. Using Palmer Penguin’s dataset \[1\], we considered which trait (flipper length or body mass) is a better predictive feature to classify  a penguin’s species.

Prior to fitting the model, we expected flipper length to be a better predictor of penguin species. This was because biologically, flippers are more distinct anatomical structures of a penguin that can mark evolutionary ancestry (hence species differentiation), compared to a flexible trait like body mass \[2\]. Also, our exploratory data analysis showed a large overlap in the body mass of Adélie and Chinstrap penguins, and we expected the machine learning model to have a harder time distinguishing between those 2 species.

Our held-out test set results with logistic regression demonstrate that flipper length is a substantially stronger single predictor of Palmer penguin species than body mass. Flipper length achieved an overall test accuracy of 0.837 and a macro-averaged F1-score of 0.715 compared to 0.744 accuracy and a 0.561 macro-averaged F1-score for body mass.  This performance gap aligns with biological differences between structural skeletal traits and pliable physiological traits in the seabirds.  Once adult penguins reach maturity, flipper length typically remains relatively stable across the breeding season, providing a consistent morphological signal across species. By contrast, body mass can fluctuate considerably depending on recent foraging success, fasting during incubation, and parental provisioning duties \[3\] introducing within species variance that blurs decision boundaries in a single-predictor logistic regression model.

Examining species-level errors reveals why overall accuracy remained below 0.85 for both single-feature classifiers. Gentoo penguins are noticeably larger in both flipper length and body mass than their congeners in the Palmer Archipelago, allowing both models to identify Gentoo individuals with high reliability. However, Adélie and Chinstrap penguins share very similar

body mass distributions, causing the body mass classifier to misclassify nearly all test-set Chinstrap penguins as Adélie. While flipper length separated Adélie and Chinstrap penguins moderately better than body mass, a single linear boundary on one morphological feature cannot fully resolve overlapping measurements between these two smaller species.

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings. First, restricting each logistic regression model to a single predictor ignores complementary morphological trait such as bill length and bill depth that strongly distinguish Chinstrap penguins from Adélie penguins. Second, the dataset exhibits class imbalance across species and spans three breeding seasons across different islands in the Palmer Archipelago \[1\] meaning environmental and inter-annual shifts in prey availability could influence body mass measurements. Third, adult penguins exhibit sexual dimorphism in body size \[3\], and pooling males and females without accounting for sex increases overlap between smaller males of one species and larger females of another. In addition, this classification is strictly machine-learning, and cannot cover the scope of correct taxonomic classification of a species.
